messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The afternoon of February 14th, 2021, was unseasonably warm, and Richard had opened the sliding glass door to let the breeze through the house. He was at his desk in the study, running spreadsheets for a client’s quarterly review, when he heard his wife Margaret call out from the garden that she needed a hand with the azaleas. He said he would be right there, finished the cell he was in, and stood up. By the time he got to the back door, she was already on the ground. The first responders said it was a massive coronary event. She was gone before she hit the dirt. Richard had knelt beside her, his hands on her face, telling her to wake up, that he was right here, that everything was fine, while the azaleas swayed in the breeze he had let into the house.

Three years later, that memory still arrives without warning. He will be sitting in a quarterly meeting, listening to a colleague present revenue projections, and suddenly he is back on the flagstone path, the smell of damp soil in his nostrils, the impossible stillness of her chest under his palm. The memory does not come as a story; it comes as a full-body event. His heart slams against his ribs, his palms go slick with sweat, and a wave of nausea rises so fast he has to grip the edge of the conference table to keep from swaying. He has learned to excuse himself to the restroom, where he stands over the sink, breathing slowly, watching his hands shake in the fluorescent light. He tells himself this is just a memory, it is not happening now, but his body does not seem to believe him.

The world has become a landscape of traps. A coworker mentions that their elderly mother passed away, and Richard feels a hot spike of rage that frightens him. He is not angry at the coworker; the anger simply arrives, sudden and overwhelming, and he has to bite the inside of his cheek to keep from saying something cutting. He has stopped attending the weekly team lunches because someone always brings up a loss, a sick pet, a dying parent, a memorial service, and he cannot predict when the switch will flip. He has also stopped driving past the cemetery where Margaret is buried, even though it is the most direct route to the grocery store. He takes a longer way now, adding fifteen minutes each way, because the sight of the iron gates and the rows of headstones sends a physical jolt through him, a clench in his gut that feels like a punch. Funerals are out of the question. He has not attended a single one since Margaret’s, not even for his own brother-in-law, who died last November. He sent flowers and a card, and he did not go.

At home, he keeps the television on news channels, loud enough to fill the silence, but he does not really watch. He has become expert at not thinking. When the memory surfaces, he forces his mind to a spreadsheet, to a column of numbers, to the precise geometry of a balance sheet. He has learned to press the thought down so quickly that sometimes he is not even sure it was there. But the price of this skill is that he feels very little else. His daughter called last week to tell him she is pregnant, and he heard himself say, “That’s nice, honey,” in a voice that sounded like it belonged to someone else. He felt nothing. He was terrified by the absence of feeling. He had come to believe that if he let himself feel the joy of her news, the grief would pour through the same crack, and he would drown.

Richard sought help because his daughter told him, gently, that she was worried about him. She said he seemed hollow. He knew she was right. He is afraid of what he has become—a man who cannot be present for a birth, who cannot sit with his own daughter’s happiness, because he has walled himself off so completely that nothing gets in. He is also afraid of what will happen if the walls come down. But he came anyway, because he does not want to be a ghost to the people he still loves.
